clinicalPearls: Consider MCTD in a patient with overlapping features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis who does not neatly fit any single diagnosis.
Puffy, swollen ('sausage') fingers and severe Raynaud phenomenon are classic early findings, often preceding other manifestations by years.
High-titer anti-U1-ribonucleoprotein (anti-U1-RNP) antibody is the serologic hallmark and is required for diagnosis.
Pulmonary arterial hypertension is the leading cause of death and can develop insidiously, so periodic screening is warranted even when patients feel well.
Esophageal dysmotility and other sclerodermoid features are common, similar to limited systemic sclerosis.
Renal disease and severe CNS involvement are less frequent than in classic SLE, but can occur and should not be dismissed.
Clinical phenotype can evolve over time, and some patients eventually reclassify into a more defined connective tissue disease such as scleroderma or SLE.
Myositis in MCTD tends to respond well to glucocorticoids compared with some other overlap myopathies.
harrison.pathophysiology: MCTD is an overlap autoimmune connective tissue disorder characterized by immune-mediated vasculopathy and fibrosis affecting skin, synovium, muscle, esophagus, lungs, and vasculature. It is strongly associated with high titers of antibody against the U1-RNP component of the spliceosome, which is thought to contribute to immune complex formation and endothelial injury. The vascular pathology, particularly intimal proliferation in pulmonary and other vessels, resembles that seen in systemic sclerosis and underlies the propensity for pulmonary arterial hypertension.
nonInfectiousMimics: Primary Raynaud phenomenon with isolated ANA positivity
additionalInvestigations: ANA with reflex extractable nuclear antigen panel — screens for anti-U1-RNP, the defining autoantibody
Anti-U1-RNP antibody titer — confirms diagnosis when present in high titer, typically without anti-Sm or anti-dsDNA
Creatine kinase and aldolase — assess for accompanying myositis
Pulmonary function tests with diffusion capacity (DLCO) — detect early interstitial lung disease or pulmonary vascular involvement
Transthoracic echocardiogram — screen for pulmonary arterial hypertension, a major prognostic driver
High-resolution chest CT — evaluate for interstitial lung disease
Esophageal manometry or barium swallow — assess for dysmotility seen in sclerodermoid overlap
Urinalysis and renal function panel — screen for renal involvement, which is less common but clinically important
redFlags: New dyspnea on exertion or signs of right heart strain suggesting evolving pulmonary arterial hypertension
Rapidly progressive proteinuria, hematuria, or rising creatinine suggesting renal involvement
Severe digital ischemia or ulceration from vasculopathy
New neurologic deficits or severe headache raising concern for CNS or cerebrovascular involvement
Acute severe muscle weakness or dysphagia suggesting active myositis with aspiration risk
pitfalls: Attributing puffy hands and Raynaud phenomenon solely to early scleroderma without checking anti-U1-RNP and considering MCTD.
Failing to screen asymptomatic patients periodically for pulmonary arterial hypertension, the dominant cause of mortality.
Assuming a single high anti-U1-RNP titer alone confirms diagnosis without correlating with the required overlapping clinical features.
Overlooking that clinical features can evolve over years, sometimes prompting reclassification into a more defined connective tissue disease.
harrison.prognosis: Overall prognosis is generally better than diffuse systemic sclerosis but variable, with outcomes largely determined by the degree of pulmonary vascular and interstitial lung involvement. Pulmonary arterial hypertension is the most significant predictor of mortality, making regular cardiopulmonary surveillance essential.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Mixed Connective Tissue Disease and Overlap Syndromes (Section on Disorders of Immune-Mediated Injury)
